title: TESS dips of 126 complex periodic variables drift by about 2e-4 cycles per rotation, do not widen and last about 130 rotations, so free orbits need radial spread below 0.04% of corotation
abstract: We test whether the material that causes complex periodic variable (CPV) dips is on free orbits or is forced to corotate, and how long one dip lasts. We fitted 15-harmonic models in short windows to all 443 TESS 2-minute light curves (2018-2026) of 126 on-target CPVs. We linked the dips into tracks and calibrated them with a fixed-shape null and with drift and shear injections. In 540 long tracks (94 stars, median 46 rotations), the median absolute drift is 1.6e-4 cycles per rotation (95%: 1.3-1.9e-4); the null gives 3e-6. Injected drifts come back with slope 0.90. Coexisting dips drift relative to each other by a median of 2.4e-4 (523 pairs). Widths do not grow systematically (69 grow, 57 narrow). Free clumps would need a fractional radial spread below 3.8e-4 (tracks longer than 80 rotations), or random speeds below about 0.1 km/s. The null-corrected mean dip life is 132 rotations (88-188), about 53 days, and longer for stronger dips. Thus free gas or dust would shear apart in a few rotations. The material is held in rigid corotation, or is replaced at fixed longitudes. The drifts are of the order of fully convective surface shear. Limitations: the window resolution limits width tests; minima can move because substructure changes; feature lives are effective values; the physical numbers use an example star.
